original_question: In a Smarandache geometry, meaning a geometry with at least one axiom that behaves in at least two different ways within the same space, and in particular in the partially Euclidean and partially non-Euclidean geometry obtained by replacing Euclid's fifth postulate with five alternative parallel behaviors, determine whether the circle equation x^2 + y^2 = r^2 still holds, and if it does, how many nontrivial solutions it has. More generally, determine whether there is a general model for all Smarandache geometries, and prove an analogue of the Archimedean triangle theorem in these multispaces.
target_in_paper: The draft mainly targets §2.9, Open Problem (i)-(ii) ('Non-Euclidean geometry by giving up the fifth postulate'), but it also folds in the separate final question of §2.10 ('Is there a general model for all Smarandache Geometries...?') and the separate open problem of §2.11 ('Non-Archimedean triangle theorem'). ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))
correct_elements: The draft correctly captures the paper’s definition-level idea that a Smarandache geometry has at least one axiom that behaves in at least two different ways within the same space, and it correctly identifies the specific partially Euclidean/partially non-Euclidean setting obtained by replacing Euclid’s fifth postulate with five alternative parallel behaviors. It also correctly reproduces the substance of the §2.9 circle question and notices the neighboring §2.10 and §2.11 questions. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))
missing_details: The draft merges three distinct open problems—§2.9 Open Problem (i)-(ii), the final question of §2.10, and §2.11—whereas the paper poses them separately. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))

For the circle and triangle-theorem questions, the relevant setting is not arbitrary Smarandache geometry, but the specific geometry of §2.9 in which there exist line/exterior-point configurations exhibiting each of the five stated parallel behaviors: exactly one parallel; finitely many parallels l1,l2,...,lk with k>2; no parallel; infinitely many but not all parallels; and all lines through the point parallel. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))

The 'general model' question belongs only to §2.10 and concerns Smarandache geometries in general; it is not presented in the paper as a consequence or extension of the §2.9 circle problem. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))

The 'rule similar to the Archimedean triangle theorem' in §2.11 is explicitly asked only for the geometry of §2.9 ('the above non-Euclidean geometry by giving up the fifth postulate'), not for all Smarandache geometries. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))

The paper introduces the terminology 'Smarandachely denied' and the notation s-point, s-line, s-plane, s-space, s-triangle, which the draft paraphrases but does not name. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))

The paper does not specify an ambient coordinate model or field for x, y, r, so a fully stand-alone rewrite should avoid silently assuming real coordinates, integer coordinates, or a specific analytic model. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))
The phrase 'nontrivial solutions' is used in §2.9 but not defined there; the draft leaves this ambiguity unresolved. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))

The paper uses the phrase 'these multispaces' in §2.11 and later notes in §2.13 that there is not much theory behind multi-space in this text, so the draft should not broaden the question into a fully developed general multispace theory beyond what the paper actually asks. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))
refined_question: Let a Smarandache geometry mean a geometry with at least one Smarandachely denied axiom, i.e. an axiom that behaves in at least two different ways within the same space. In the specific geometry of §2.9 obtained by replacing Euclid’s fifth postulate so that, for suitable choices of a line and an exterior point, the parallel axiom can occur in each of the five ways listed there—exactly one parallel, finitely many k>2 parallels, no parallel, infinitely many but not all parallels, and all lines through the point parallel—determine whether the circle equation x^2 + y^2 = r^2 remains valid; if it does, determine how many nontrivial solutions it has. For this same multispacial geometry, determine whether there is a rule analogous to the Archimedean triangle theorem and prove the corresponding theorem. Separately, for Smarandache geometries in general, determine whether there exists a single general model from which particular Smarandache geometries can be recovered by varying parameters.
justification: The paper’s actual intent here is a cluster of nearby but distinct open questions. Section 2.9 asks, for the particular 'non-Euclidean geometry by giving up the fifth postulate,' whether the circle equation x^2+y^2=r^2 still holds and, if so, how many nontrivial solutions it has. Section 2.10 then steps back, defines Smarandache geometry and asks a different question: whether there is a general model for all Smarandache geometries obtained by changing parameters. Section 2.11 returns to the geometry of §2.9 and asks for a rule analogous to the Archimedean triangle theorem in 'these multispaces.' A faithful rewrite therefore has to preserve both the specific §2.9 geometry and the fact that the §2.10 and §2.11 questions are separate, not a single generalized theorem request. The paper does not add a formal coordinate field, a definition of 'nontrivial solutions,' or a rigorous general multispace formalism in this neighborhood, so the refined question should not invent them. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))
